parts.text: Jack’s fingers slipped from the ledge,
parts.meaning: Jack's fingers slid off the narrow shelf of rock,

parts.text: but Annie held on to his wrist with both hands
parts.meaning: but Annie kept holding his wrist with two hands

parts.text: as he dangled high above the stony ground below.
parts.meaning: while he hung high over the rocky ground.

sentences.grammar: "But" shows the second thing is good news after bad news. "Hold on to" = keep holding. "As" = while.

sentences.context: He tried not to think about running out of time, or losing their rock-climbing skills, or the danger in the dark valley.
sentences.simple: Jack tried to stop thinking about three bad things: having no time left, losing their climbing power, and the danger in the dark valley.
sentences.main: He tried not to think about these things.

parts.text: He tried not to think about
parts.meaning: Jack tried to stop thinking about

parts.text: running out of time,
parts.meaning: having no more time,

parts.text: or losing their rock-climbing skills,
parts.meaning: or losing their power to climb rocks,

parts.text: or the danger in the dark valley.
parts.meaning: or the danger in the dark valley.

sentences.grammar: "Try not to do" = try to stop yourself doing something. After "about", we use -ing forms ("running", "losing") or nouns ("the danger").

sentences.context: He tried to block out the pain in his arm and shoulder by closing his eyes and concentrating on the sounds of the night.
sentences.simple: Jack tried not to feel the pain in his arm and shoulder. He closed his eyes and listened carefully to the night sounds.
sentences.main: He tried to block out the pain.

parts.text: He tried to block out the pain in his arm and shoulder
parts.meaning: Jack tried to stop feeling the pain in his arm and shoulder

parts.text: by closing his eyes and concentrating on the sounds of the night.
parts.meaning: by shutting his eyes and thinking only about the night sounds.

sentences.grammar: "By + -ing" tells how you do something. "Block out" = stop something from reaching you, here the pain.

sentences.context: “I appreciate your gratitude, children, but an ankle bandage and a simple arm sling should not convince you I will be a great nurse.”
sentences.simple: Florence says: "Thank you for saying thank you. But fixing an ankle and an arm does not show that I will be a great nurse."
sentences.main: An ankle bandage and an arm sling should not convince you.

parts.text: “I appreciate your gratitude, children,
parts.meaning: "Thank you for thanking me, children,

parts.text: but an ankle bandage and a simple arm sling
parts.meaning: but one bandage on an ankle and one easy sling for an arm

parts.text: should not convince you I will be a great nurse.”
parts.meaning: should not make you sure I will be a great nurse."

sentences.grammar: "Convince you (that) ..." = make you believe something; "that" is left out. "Should not" here means it is not a good reason.

sentences.context: I must do more than walk around the garden, write meaningless letters, sit in drawing rooms, gossip about the neighbors, arrange flowers, and go to dances!
sentences.simple: Florence says she must do more with her life than the small things rich ladies do every day, like letters, visits, flowers and dances.
sentences.main: I must do more than these things!

parts.text: I must do more than
parts.meaning: I need to do more with my life than

parts.text: walk around the garden, write meaningless letters, sit in drawing rooms,
parts.meaning: walk in the garden, write letters that mean nothing, sit in sitting rooms,

parts.text: gossip about the neighbors, arrange flowers, and go to dances!
parts.meaning: talk about the neighbors, put flowers in vases, and go to dances!

sentences.grammar: "Do more than + base verb": after "more than" the list uses base verbs (walk, write, sit, gossip, arrange, go). This long list shows how boring her life feels.

sentences.context: As they followed Florence out of her cabin, dawn was spreading its rosy glow across the Temple of Luxor, the anchored sailboats, and the waters of the Nile.
sentences.simple: They walked out of Florence's room on the boat behind her. The early morning sun was putting a pink light over the temple, the boats and the river.
sentences.main: Dawn was spreading its rosy glow.

parts.text: As they followed Florence out of her cabin,
parts.meaning: While they walked out of the cabin behind Florence,

parts.text: dawn was spreading its rosy glow
parts.meaning: the early morning was sending its pink light

parts.text: across the Temple of Luxor, the anchored sailboats, and the waters of the Nile.
parts.meaning: over the temple, the boats and the river Nile.

sentences.grammar: The writer talks about dawn like a person: dawn "spreads its glow". "Was spreading" (past continuous) shows it was happening while they walked out.

sentences.context: His whole opinion of Florence had changed since she had tended to their injuries so kindly and he had heard her speak about her dreams.
sentences.simple: Jack now thought about Florence in a new way. She had cared for their hurt bodies so kindly, and he had heard her talk about her dreams.
sentences.main: His whole opinion of Florence had changed.

parts.text: His whole opinion of Florence had changed
parts.meaning: Jack's ideas about Florence were now all different

parts.text: since she had tended to their injuries so kindly
parts.meaning: after she cared for their wounds very kindly

parts.text: and he had heard her speak about her dreams.
parts.meaning: and after he heard her talk about her dreams.

sentences.grammar: "Had changed", "had tended", "had heard" are the past perfect: these things happened before the time of the story. "Heard her speak" = heard + person + base verb.

sentences.context: Her wealthy, upper-class family wanted her to marry and become “a proper society lady,” but Florence wanted to help others and become a professional nurse.
sentences.simple: Her rich family wanted her to marry and be a fine lady, but Florence wanted to help people and work as a nurse.
sentences.main: Her family and Florence wanted different things.

parts.text: Her wealthy, upper-class family wanted her to marry and become “a proper society lady,”
parts.meaning: Her rich, important family wanted her to marry and be a fine lady,

parts.text: but Florence wanted to help others and become a professional nurse.
parts.job: What Florence wanted ("but" shows the difference).
parts.meaning: but Florence wanted to help people and work as a trained nurse.

sentences.grammar: "Wanted her to marry" = want + person + to + verb. "But" joins two opposite ideas.

burn up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

close by.example: The jackals must be close by, Jack thought.
close by.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.
